speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There are two amendments; that was the first.

I just want to say a word or two with regard to the first amendment.
I am aware that all these bills must contain provisions granting power to make regulations, but I always protest at such extreme power being taken. It gets down to the point where the governor in council instead of this parliament is given power to legislate. On page 2 the bill states:
such advances shall be made under regulations established from time to time by the governor in council-
The other day the Minister of Finance introduced a bill in connection with loaning money to municipalities, and he safeguarded

Indian Act
himself by repeated conditions. He said the rate of interest was to be two per cent; that no single municipality could get more than so much, and so on; but all these powers in this case are to be exercised by the governor in council. Is any interest to be charged on these loans? We do not know. Surely we ought to know. If we were dealing with white people I am sure we would be demanding that information. Then again, is there to be a limit; is any one Indian or any one band to be allowed to get a large amount, or is there to be a restriction such as the Minister of Finance provided in his bill? Then again, is there to be any period to the making of these loans? Is it to extend for all time or for a limited time, or what are these conditions?
I submit that we ought to be informed on these points, and that these matters should not be left to be dealt with by regulation. I submit that the general outline of these things should be put in the bill. Surely it is not out of the way that anyone representing Indians, as we all do indirectly, should ask whether they are to pay interest and, if so, at what rate. Is there to be any amortization? If so, what is the period? I think we are entitled to know all these things. Does the minister not think so also?
Mr. CRERaR: The purpose of the provision in the section which my hon. friend has just criticized is really to limit the power of the department; in other words, the con-* ditions under which these loans may be made or advances given, and the uses to which this revolving fund may be put, will not lie wholly within the discretion of the Indian department but will have to conform to regulations adopted by the governor in council. That is the purpose of the provision.
So far as the rates of interest are com-cerned, certainly it would be the [DOT] intention to charge interest, but the rate might vary in certain cases. For instance, a certain rate of interest might be charged to an individual Indian; another rate of interest charged on a loan to an Indian school for the purchase of materials to be worked up into goods for sale. Those conditions should not be too rigid. I repeat that the purpose of this provision is to not leave the power wholly in the Indian department to say when or how or to whom these advances may be made out of this fund, but to subject that to the scrutiny and approval of the governor in council. It may be necessary to vary the conditions from time to time, and that is why provision is made to vest the governor in council with power to make these regulations.

I really do not accept with any intense appreciation the explanation given. The minister says the real purpose of giving the governor in council this power to legislate by regulation is to prevent too much power getting into the hands of the department; that now the matter will be controlled by regulations which must be approved by the governor in council. Of course that does not sound so bad, but while I have never been in the council I have an idea that these regulations will be prepared by his department and presented by him to council more or less as a matter of form. Then it will be held in council that as the minister whose department is concerned has gone into the matter thoroughly and prepared these regulations, they must be appropriate, and they will go through as a matter of course. What I am suggesting is that it should not be left to the governor in council to settle these things; they should be settled by this house, as was done in the case of the housing act, the farm lean act and so on. which had to do with white men. I cannot see why an Indian, or those interested in the welfare of the Indians, should be kept more in the dark, than those concerned with white people.
The minister says he does not know what rate of interest will be charged. That is an extraordinary statement. We are going to embark upon what seems to me a hazardous enterprise if we charge varying rates to different people. Why should Jones get a better rate than Smith? I cannot see why. I should suppose that the interest charged either of them would be governed to some extent at least by the interest the government has to pay in the first place, as is the case under the farm loan act. That board has to sell its debentures, and they must loan the money to the farmers at a certain interest rate not more than so much above the rate they have to pay. But now this matter is going to be dealt with by regulation, and the interest may be varied according to the circumstances. I do not know why one Indian should get a better rate than another. An Indian can easily make up a story as to why his circumstances are more necessitous than those of the other man, or why a school should be favoured more than a band of Indians, and so on.
I agree with what the right hon. leader of the opposition said as to the inadvisability of lending money to individual Indians, because if you do you will not be bothered about interest, repayments or anything like that; you will not get back more than two per

Indian Act

cent anyway. However, I do think the committee should be informed on these matters. The minister has not told us the rate of interest he is going to charge, but that will be dealt with by regulation under the act. I really do suggest that it is not desirable to give the governor in council, which largely means the department, such sweeping powers, such as are not asserted by the Minister of Finance, whose department is supposedly much more capable in these matters than the Indian department. I should like the minister to express himself as to whether he does not think it advisable that at least there should be some indication as to the interest to be charged, the period for which it is to be charged and the limitations in regard to individual loans. Can he not give us any information on those points?

No; at the moment I am not in a position to give my hon. friend information on those points. As a matter of fact, the farm loan act, the home improvement act and the Dominion Housing Act all give power to make the necessary regulations for the carrying out of the acts. This is a new venture, wholly in the nature of an experiment-I think with a fair chance of working out-and I do not think it is asking too much to give the governor in council power to make regulations for the administration of this fund. We could have left out that provision, in which case the administration of the fund would have remained wholly in the hands of the Indian department. Obviously that might be open to criticism. I can assure my hon. friend that while I may bring or recommend to council certain regulations under this act, that does not at all mean that council will accept my proposals,

Yes. That was really a mistake, though. The right hon. leader of the opposition is getting a good deal of merriment out of that typographical error, but I can assure him that his guess in that respect is just as wide of the mark as many of his guesses in connection with other matters.
If his other guesses were as accurate as this he has been correct very often.

No; he is wide of the mark. Those are the reasons why we suggest that the governor in council should be given power to make regulations. They may limit the loans and say, " You cannot go above a certain amount in individual cases."

What amount?
I Mr. Neill.]
That will be determined by the circumstances of the case.

That is what I am objecting to; we are giving the government power to legislate. I protest that we are passing a bill which we would not pass if it were to apply to white men. The minister says the other acts give power to make regulations. That is so, but it is subject to the other provisions of the bills which set the rates of interest. Is the rate of interest in this case to be one per cent or 6 per cent or 10 per cent, or what is it to be? Is this a proper provision for us to pass? The minister says he does not think there is going to be any harm done. If we are to surrender to the governor in council our power to legislate, let us understand it; but why does not the Minister of Finance do it? I may say any experience I have had with the Indian department in recent years would encourage me to put power into the hands of the Minister of Finance rather than into those of the Department of Indian Affairs.
But that was prior to 1935.

We will not go into dates. But I do submit the minister has not given us satisfactory reasons why we should pass legislation giving his department power- because it comes down to that; his recommendation is accepted by council-to fix a rate of interest which is entirely in the air. Will he say it will not exceed 6 per cent? When the bill in connection with farm loans was before the house we asked the questions: What is the farmer to pay? What rate wilt he be charged? What is the service charge to be?
Is there to be amortization in this instance, and over how many years is it to be spread? I think we are entitled to know these things before we pass legislation of this kind? The minister is content to say, " It is an experiment." Yes, but let us limit the experiment to within at least reasonable bounds.
There is one other matter I should like to discuss, although it does not apply directly to the bill. It was introduced by the minister. When he spoke on the resolution he referred to band funds, and indicated that those funds belonged to the bands and therefore could not be used for purposes suggested in the bill. His actual words were:
As a matter of fact, when these moneys go into the band funds, they cannot be taken out of the band funds by the administration without the consent of the Indians.
If he had put that into the bill I would be very happy, because I have been trying to get

Indian Act
that provision for many years. When I was Indian agent I would at times be sent to get the surrender of a piece of land from Indians to be used for necessary purposes, such as the building of a railway, or something of that kind. The first thing the Indians would say was-and I need not put it into dialect- "What are we getting out of this?" I would say, "The law says you are getting a certain sum of money, half of which will be distributed among you, and the other half put into a fund in your name." Although they did not ask it at first, later they did ask, "What is the fund going to be used for?" Later on they discovered, and I discovered, that this was used to pay relief to the Indians, and the Indians-not being absolute fools-when I came back again to get another surrender said. "What is the advantage in our surrendering this piece of land? We give up a piece of our land, and you take the equivalent, in money and put it into a fund. We understand that. You keep it in a bank. Then, when our people are poor and when we go on relief you take the money out of our fund. If we had not given the surrender of that piece of land we would still have enjoyed relief. But now you make us pay our relief out of our capital. You have persuaded us to surrender this land. We receive only half the sum in cash, and now you pay the rest into the fund and it is used to pay relief." They said-and they used a strong word- "you allow the department to rob us of that money." The same policy is still going on in a greater or lesser degree. If the bill is to provide for funds to lend the Indians money, and if the minister says that, as a matter of fact, when these Indian moneys go into the band funds they cannot be taken out without the consent of the band, then it is all right with me. But that is not by any means the policy the department has carried out.

I really think that on reflection the minister will realize that it is desirable to state, say 3 per cent interest. I concur in the views expressed by the hon. member for Comox-Albemi.
Just let us pause for a minute. If it is going to be open to differentiation between east and west, we are going to have the same difficulties that governments have experienced in times past. That is the reason why I take it that in the measure before us yesterday there was provision for a 2 per cent rate, but it applied equally to the west and to the east. It applied to every part of Canada; and I should think that if the minister provided for possibly 3 per cent, he would be fair to the Indians, having regard to the nature of the experiment, and to the countrv.
I can only say, of course, that the minister knows how fully I agree with the observations of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni as to the governor in council becoming a legislative rather than an administrative body. There are measures which are quasi-administrative and quasi-legislative in regard to which the executive must at all times have jurisdiction, and exercise it. Here you are dealing in a legislative way with matters which during the present session and in previous sessions we have thought of sufficient importance to be dealt with by parliament, and not by the delegated authority which the governor in council receives from parliament.
I think the minister would be well advised to consider, and favourably, the suggestion made by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, and provide for a 3 per cent rate. Then there would be no difficulty between contending communities as to the rate. The minister would say, "It is fixed by statute: I cannot make it more or less. It is the same in Ontario as it is in British Columbia." I believe he would find this very satisfactory.
There is no danger of conflict between contending communities in the administration of this provision.
There might be.

I do not wish to place
upon it the limitation suggested by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. It may be desirable in certain circumstances to loan money for a certain period free of interest altogether. For instance, we may wish to take up the matter of making handicraft articles for sale, and as an encouragement to an Indian school we might say, "We will advance you a few thousand dollars"-or a few hundred dollars, as the case may be- "to buy material out of which you may make these goods." There may be another instance where we would be advancing money to an Indian tribe as a whole for the purchase of live stock, a project which would be of common interest to the tribe. In that case we might wish to charge 4 per cent or 5 per cent. If we put in a definite provision setting out that a certain rate of interest will be charged, I believe we will make the administration too rigid and too difficult.
I should be very glad indeed if I might believe that the hon. member for Comox-Alberni had a little more confidence in the impartiality and fairness of the government in protecting the public interest in connection with making these regulations. I believe this might be very well assumed in the circumstances.
*>1052-221i
Indian Act

It is the judgment of the
Indian department I am dubious about.

I promise the hon. member for Comox-Alberni that as always I shall scrutinize carefully any recommendation I make to council in connection with a matter of this kind. I should like to agree to the suggestion of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, but I think it would be a handicap in administration.

I assume we must accept
the minister's statement and must not waste more time in the discussion, but I must point out that this is a most extraordinary situation, one which has never been seen in the house before, where large sums are being loaned without the rate of interest being indicated. However, let it go at that.

I do not think they
can collect any.

And it is discriminatory.
One man can get it at one rate, and another body such as a church or some body with possibly more political influence,, can get it at another. The Minister of Finance is now in his seat. May I say to him that I was paying him a compliment by stating that when he introduced legislation in connection with a large loan he insisted that the rate of interest, the amount of amortization, the period of the loan, limitations as to municipalities, and so on, be defined in the bill. I do not know whether the minister's attention has been called to it, but here is a bill under which we are told it is proposed to lend up to $350,000 at varying rates of interest.
I stated it might be desirable to vary the minimum, or it might be useful.

I had in mind the bills the Minister of Finance introduced in connection with farmers' creditors and so on. In those bills the minister always defined the rates of interest, the charges and so on. However, the Minister of Mines and Resources will not accept this suggestion. I just want to make one last suggestion, that there should be a concluding section in this bill similar to that which appears in many bills, that within fifteen days after the opening of parliament a report shall be made covering the preceding calendar year. That would make the information readily available for us during the session.
I would be quite prepared to accept that suggestion.
I am astonished.

The hon. member for Comox-Alberni is making headway. If he continues he will have the whole bill redrafted according to his wishes. However, speaking seriously, I think his suggestion is a useful one. Perhaps this section could stand also, and the hon. member's suggestion will be incorporated in the bill.

speechtext:
Mr.	LIONEL CHEVRIER	(Stormont)
(for Mr. Martin) moved the second reading of Bill No. 124 to amend the Copyright Act.

subtopic: POWER OF MINISTER TO PROTECT PUBLIC AGAINST ABUSES OF EXCLUSIVE RIGHTS
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: POWER OF MINISTER TO PROTECT PUBLIC AGAINST ABUSES OF EXCLUSIVE RIGHTS
speechtext:
The sponsor of this bill, the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) is unavoidably absent this evening, and has asked me to speak to this motion. The present Copyright Act contains provision for relief where the owner of the copyright fails to print a copyrighted work or cause the same to be printed in Canada, or fails to supply the reasonable demands of the Canadian market for such work. In such case any person may apply to the Secretary of State for a licence to print the work. The granting of the application is subject to various conditions. The compulsory licence provisions are limited to domestic works where the author is a Canadian citizen. The purpose of the present bill, as I understand, is to give to the minister greater powers in dealing with such applications and to protect the public against any abuse of the exclusive rights conferred upon copyright owners by the act. The further powers conferred by the bill correspond with the powers given by similar provisions under the Patent Act, 1935. It is the intention of the sponsor of this bill to amend it in committee so that application may in future be made not to the minister but to the registrar of patents, and also that the relief may be granted by the registrar of patents. It also provides for leave to appeal from his decision to the exchequer

Copyright Act
court of Canada within a certain period of time, so that such applications will ultimately be reviewed by the courts.
The present bill arises out of a decision of the minister holding that under the present working of the compulsory licence sections of the Copyright Act he had no jurisdiction to grant an application for a compulsory licence in connection with certain fire insurance maps which are the subject of copyright. This application had the support, among others, of thirty-three Canadian fire insurance companies, but the minister was unable under the present wording of the section to consider the application on its merits. The bill is obviously one which should be considered by a standing committee, and it strikes me that the committee on banking and commerce is the one to which it should be referred.

subtopic: POWER OF MINISTER TO PROTECT PUBLIC AGAINST ABUSES OF EXCLUSIVE RIGHTS
speechtext:
Perhaps in the absence of the hon. member who introduced this bill I may now give a further explanation as to its motive and what it may lead to. I must congratulate my friend, the hon. member for Stormont (Mr. Chevrier) who in a few words has given the essential features of this bill. Its object is to introduce into the Copyright Act sections similar to those which already exist in the Patent Act, permitting the minister to grant redress in the case of monopolistic ownership of a copyright. This provision does not exist in the Copyright Act, and the reason is quite obvious. I majr point out that in the Patent Act there are a number of sections which are fairly sweeping, whereby in case of abuse of rights under patents the commissioner of patents may order the owner of the patent to supply the Canadian market, and a complete series of sections provide that the patent owner may appeal to the exchequer court, etcetera. These sections are Nos. 65, 66, 67, 68 and 69 and other sections of the Patent Act of 1935.
There is an essential difference between a patent and a copyright. By reference to the interpretation section of the Patent Act one finds an invention defined as "any new and useful art, process, machine, manufacture or composition of matters, or any new and useful improvement in any art, process, machine, manufacture or composition of matter.'' In other words, the Patent Act deals with an object, and gives an exclusive right to a patentee to manufacture and sell that object. A copyright is a different thing. The definition of copyright is found in section 3 of chapter 32 of the Revised Statutes of Canada, 1927:-
For the purposes of this act, "copyright" means the sole right to produce or reproduce the work or any substantial part thereof in
any material form whatsoever, to perform, or in the case of a lecture to deliver, the work or any substantial part thereof in public; if the work is unpublished, to publish the work or any substantial part thereof.
I think it is apparent, when those two definitions are compared, that a copyright is quite a different thing from a patent. In the case of a copyright, which covers mostly works of a literary or artistic nature, it has never appeared that the owner of a copyright could have the least interest in not publishing or selling reproductions of the work therefore there has been no provision made in the Copyright Act, and to my knowledge- and I have been following copyright discussions for the last twenty years-this is the first instance of a demand being made, at least in the house, for a provision similar to that in the Patent Act against the monopolistic ownership of a patent.
The situation which now faces us is different altogether. Experience has shown that not only may we have to deal with an artistic or literary work, but there might also be copyrighted works of a commercial application, of which the exclusive ownership might become of great advantage to the owner of the copyright. That is the case which has been submitted recently to the Department of the Secretary of State, in which a group of insurance men are the owners of a copyright covering insurance maps which have no literary or artistic value, but which have an exceptional commercial value. In their refusal to allow another group of insurance men to buy copies of those maps they were put in a position of imposing conditions whereby these maps might be acquired by the other group, which has led to the charge against the first group of exercising a monopoly. Therefore the case has been submitted to the Secretary of State. After very careful consideration of such case, and without pronouncing on the merits but merely considering whether there is in the Copyright Act any section that might apply, my officers and I have come to the conclusion that there is none. There are, it is true, the licence clauses of the Copyright Act of 1921, but they do not apply to a case like this. I remember distinctly when these clauses were inserted. That was done under the late Hon. Mr. Doherty, and I was a member of the committee which dealt with the act at that time. I know very well that the purpose of these clauses was altogether different from the purpose that is now invoked. It was also the legal opinion of the departmental experts that these licence clauses could not possibly apply to such a monopoly.

I may add that at the time the authors protested vigorously against the insertion of these clauses in the Copyright Act, as they object also to the amendment now before the house, because they claim that copyright is an exclusive right. When the case was submitted to the department my only function was to decide as to whether the licence clauses could apply to the ownership of those insurance maps, and it is quite apparent to anyone who reads these clauses carefully that they do not. In brief, the licence clauses merely state that when a book or a work of art is edited outside Canada and the Canadian market is not supplied with copies of the work, then the printer may apply to the Secretai-y of State and obtain permission to publish the same work in Canada under certain conditions. That is why this bill is introduced now, because I think both parties are quite agreed- or at least they have to abide by the decision of the Department of the Secretary of State- that there is nothing in the present Copyright Act which deals with the particular case that has been submitted to us. Therefore, under the terms of the present act we have to decide that the owners of the copyright have exclusive rights to it and cannot be forced to sell it to anybody.
The intention of the present bill is to give the minister power to decide that in certain cases the owners of a copyright carry it to abuse, and to grant such relief, in the words of the bill, as the minister may deem just

and fair in the circumstances. Without any desire to criticize, I am afraid the bill has been drafted rather hurriedly.	I am not

subtopic: POWER OF MINISTER TO PROTECT PUBLIC AGAINST ABUSES OF EXCLUSIVE RIGHTS
speechtext:
I was coming to that. This particular phase of the question was not before the court, but the ownership of the copyright itself has been disputed and the case has been heard in the exchequer court. That court has rendered a judgment, and an appeal has been taken to the Supreme Court of Canada, so that phase of the matter is now sub judine
For all these reasons I agree with the hon. member for Stormont that we should not, in the single hour that is available twice a week for the consideration of public bills, and at this late stage of the session, endeavour to consider in detail a bill of such complexity, but that it would be much better to have some committee of the house consecrate the necessary time to it. I still have my doubts as to whether or not the principle of the bill should be adopted. speechtext:
We are now getting to the point where we propose to license transportation facilities. That is what this means. We have created transport companies on sea, land and in the air. Now we are carrying bureaucracy one step farther and providing for the licensing of organizations which under the act will transport goods and/or passengers.
To lay a foundation for a licence for that purpose is not an easy undertaking, but those who propound the measure must be prepared to support that thesis. While I have not followed in detail the work before the committee, the minister and those who hold similar views, namely the supporters of the administration, believe that a case for licensing has been made out. I am not unmindful of the difficulties that we have in this country with respect to our railways and their revenues, and the difficulties that are being experienced by the railways in other ways as well. But it is a long, far cry from financial
Transport Commission

conditions to the point where we say that we shall licence those whom we have created for the purpose of carrying on the business.
I know how strongly this has been advocated in certain quarters, and I understand their motives, motives which are sincere and earnest. They are endeavouring to increase their revenues. And they propose to increase their revenues by diminishing the traffic that is handled on the one hand by unlicensed organizations, and by increasing the traffic, they believe, of those whom they say are entitled to the licences, namely, their own organizations and others, including those operating in the air.
The section is explicit in stating that you have to determine, first, "public convenience and necessity". That is the purpose as indicated by the bill. The board of transport commissioners will have to determine whether the public convenience and necessity-it is not alternative, but is a cumulative expression-require this transport service. That issue goes before the board of transport commissioners.
If you left the issue just at that point alone, it would be rather a difficult problem. But it is rendered more difficult still; for the board is given directions as to certain factors which must be considered in determining that issue. Those factors are stated in sub-clauses to the bill, one of which refers to complaints by competitors, to put it shortly. That is number one. The board will consider the attitude of the competitors to the competing applicant organization, whether by rail, water or air, "on the routes or between the places which the applicant intends to serve on the ground that suitable facilities are or, if the licence were issued, would be in excess of requirements, or on the ground that any of the conditions of any other transport licence held by the applicant have not been complied with."
Mr. Chairman, think how splendid it. would have been if we had had a provision such as that in 'Canada, say when we built some of our present railway lines! But you see, we have these railway lines. One of the factors being considered by a senate committee to-day is that we have three transcontinental lines in certain sections of the country, merging into two as they pass through the mountains. This is locking the door after the horse has been taken from the stable. You will observe I use milder language than is usually used in connection with that proverb.
The second factor is this;
(b) whether or not the issue of such licence would tend to develop the complementary rather than the competitive functions of the different forms of transport, if any, involved in such objections.
[Mr. Brnnett.l
That is, would there be an elimination of competition? It is not for me to say at the moment whether or not that is sound, but it contemplates the granting of a licence to an applicant if his proposed methods of transport are complementary to and not competitive with existing facilities. The third one is quite comprehensive. Paragraph (c) reads:
(e) the general effect on other transport services and any public interest which may be affected by the issue of such licence.
That is involved in the broad principle which has to be determined by the board on every reference. The next paragraph deals with the quality and permanence of the service to be offered by the applicant, his financial responsibility and so on. The questions of safety in the air and matters of that kind are next dealt with. I pass these by because they are matters which we would expect anj board would have to consider. Then comes this provision:
Notwithstanding anything contained in subsection one of this section, if evidence is offered to prove,-
(a)	that during the period of twelve months next preceding the coming into force of the relative part of this act on, in or in respect of the sea or inland waters of Canada, or the route between specified points or places in Canada or between specified points or places in Canada and specified points or places outside of Canada, or the part of Canada to which the application for a licence relates, the applicant was bona fide engaged in the business of transport, and
(b)	that the applicant was during such period using ships or aircraft, as the ease may be, for the purpose of such business-
I take it that the effect of that is to have the board consider the existing facilities and conditions and the length of time during which they have been operating. Then it is provided further:
The board shall, if . satisfied with such proof, accept the same as evidence of public convenience and necessity to the extent of the user so proved and issue a licence accordingly.
This section has been changed in part since the bill went to the committee. I shall not say more than that these provisions apply largely to the inland waters, the air and the sea and do not deal with other branches of the transport service. It is a recognition of an existing right based upon and determined by the method applied in the utilization of that right by the protester during a period of twelve months prior to the date of application.
It is a little difficult to determine whether or not in a young country like this we should undertake to license these facilities. I am told by those who are deeply interested

Transport Commission
in the problem that we should likely agree to it; that it is sound. I know that they have been endeavouring to do it in the United States for a long time, but thus far they have failed. They are watching this experiment with great interest. I made some inquiries myself, and I had inquiries made by others. I believe Mr. Eastman is the gentleman who is undertaking to correlate the activities of the railways of the United States. Without trying in any sense to repeat his language, I was fold that at a public hearing he made the observation that they were watching with much interest what might happen in this country. If we were less poor as a country, the situation would be less difficult. I am not talking of our physical assets; I am talking of our accumulated material resources.
I cannot but think it is taking a rather long leap in the dark to apply to this extent the theory of bureaucracy to transport. I apprehend the answer that will be made. I should not anticipate the answer, but I have tried to think of it fairly. It is felt that this may do something to improve the financial position of our transport companies. The last paragraph to which I directed attention applies to the sea and to the air. I know the apprehension that exists among some of our friends on the prairies as to the possibilities of increased freight rates for the movement of grain from the great lakes. Whether or not that apprehension is based upon any real appreciation of the problem, time alone will demonstrate.
The minister is of the opinion that this can be faced with equanimity, without fear as to the possible results. I suppose the answer he will make is the answer that ministers always make:	If it does not work out
satisfactorily, it can always be repealed. But nations cannot make experiments as easily as individuals without paying a pretty long price. We are paying a heavy price for some of the experiments we made in Canada in days gone by when we believed that something would happen that did not happen. In other words, we predicated our views of the future upon an anticipated expansion which did not develop. The minister will observe that I am not speaking with, shall I say. my usual certainty. There is grave uncertainty in my mind, but I cannot think I would be doing justice to the situation if I adopted the principle without pointing out what I concede to be the difficulties, and my real fear of the consequences.
I believe that a planned economy may be very necessary under new conditions in many parts of the world. I am making that confession of faith at once. I believe that
the vast accumulation of knowledge which has come to mankind during the ages cannot be utilized unless by some planned utilization of the accumulated skill that comes to people only by reason of planning their operations, whatever they may be. But to plan in this instance, without its being part of a further plan, that is, a general plan, is to set up one branch of a bureaucracy without correlating its activities to a planned or logical scheme for the whole. Until such time as we are ready to contemplate that feature of our national life, it seems to me that making this gesture will not accomplish what the minister so earnestly desires.
I suppose there is no member of this committee who is not as anxious as the minister that our difficulties should find a favourable and successful solution. But it is a great responsibility to attempt regimentation with respect to our transportation services without correlating it to a planned and considered scheme that contemplates the application of the accumulated scientific and other knowledge of our world to the economic affairs of the country. I have expressed very vaguely what is in the back of my mind, but I felt that I should make these observations before I became a party to the adoption of a principle which is far more than the application of it. In the application we find that we are touching every phase of our national life. Transportation is very important from every angle, whether it be the transportation of passengers through the air, on the sea or across the land, or the movement of our freight in any way that the act contemplates and has provided for.
I can readily understand how one who represents a constituency in British Columbia looks with the greatest apprehension on a measure of this kind because British Columbia is peculiarly situated. There is transport by water, which passes through a foreign country to reach the Atlantic coast by traversing a part of the Pacific, and the utilization of a canal that has been provided at an enormous expense. So this becomes a matter of vital importance to the people of the seaport areas of British Columbia. Their ship-borne traffic passing through the canal goes not only to the markets of Europe but also to our own eastern Canada, which makes it very important from that angle also, so that if we are to license these enterprises in this way I think we might perhaps have taken a little longer time to determine whether or not in practice it would effect the benefits which the minister desires without inconveniences and disadvantages that may amount almost to a calamity in connection with the nation as a whole.

Mr. Chairman, it seems to me that the discussion of this bill brings out enormous inconsistencies. I have followed this legislation now for the second year in this chamber and in another chamber, and the inconsistency of the discussion is perhaps the chief feature of it. We have to-day the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) before dinner expressing the greatest concern lest there should be any relaxation whatsoever of regulation as applied to the railways. The regulation of the railways was applied at a time when the railways had a virtual monopoly of transportation in this country. To-day they are far from occupying that position. The purpose of this bill is to meet the changed situation by making a move in the direction of equality of opportunity for competition. Having relaxed the regulations applied to the railways, we desire to extend these relaxed regulations to those competing forms of transport over which the federal government has jurisdiction. Strangely enough, those who are most opposed to any relaxation of the regulation of the railways seem to be the ones most fearful of evil results following from the application of such relaxed regulation of ether forms of transport.
May I point out another inconsistency? Something has been said about the senate investigation. On the walls of the committee room where that discussion is taking place is a map of Canada. On that map about five thousand miles of railway are covered with a black tape, being lines that it is proposed to abandon. I think that is a fair indication in railway circles, at least, that we have too much railway transportation. On the great lakes during the last year, when traffic was light, we have had some forty lake boats scrapped simply because there were no cargoes for them. There is actually to-day an impending shortage of tonnage on the great lakes, and the fact that freight rates on grain from the head of the lakes to Montreal have advanced from four cents to 5J cents a bushel during this season is an indication of changed conditions that exist there.

[Mr. Bennett.J
is uneconomical for any country, and that the shippers of the country would be better and more cheaply served if it were not necessary for the transportation industry to have a surplus of transport facilities. The public pays for those facilities in the end, and while in times of depression there may be abnormally cheap transportation, in times of large production the price is apt to go to a point which will bring a fair average return on the surplus facilities.
We believe-and other countries have shared that view, because the principle of convenience and necessity is of widespread application as applied to transportation facilities- that it is desirable to give the regulating board the privilege of deciding whether an increase in our transportation facilities is required by public convenience and necessity. This bill proposes that we attempt to make some progress in the direction of relaxation of the regulation of the railways, on the one hand, and that we extend regulation to unregulated carriers, on the other. I think everything in the bill indicates that we are instructing the board of transport commissioners to apply the new regulations cautiously. The board has behind it fifty years of experience in regulating transportation as a background for extending its operations, and I believe that no harm can be done by the application of this bill to transportation in Canada. I believe, on the contrary, that considerable good can be accomplished by a wise application of the provisions of this bill.
I find it difficult to understand why many people are very timid about placing this bill on the statute books. People talk very freely about drastic solutions of the railway problem. But think of the havoc that would follow the tearing up of any five thousand miles of railway in this country, and compare that with any disabilities to the Canadian people that could arise from this bill, and in comparison the latter must appear very trivial indeed. speechtext:
I am sure the minister
will acquit me of any desire to take up too much time. This matter has been thoroughly discussed in the committee and I have no desire to trespass upon their good will. But I think I should point out to him that he is in error when he speaks of inconsistency; he has failed to grasp the essential underlying foundation of the argument addressed to the committee. It will be remembered that after a long struggle the masses of the people secured equality under the law with respect to freight rates. That was a very long struggle. All one has to do in order to get a clear appreciation of the nature of that struggle is to read casually the history of transportation in the United States. And in our own country we followed that old statement of Commodore Vanderbilt that freight rates were based upon all the traffic could stand, and that the large shipper who had a tremendous volume of trade for the railways could get a rate denied to the small man who was endeavouring to start a very indifferent business. That principle was swept away. That fact is at the basis of our whole railway law on the traffic side of it, and the change in the United States was secured after infinite struggle. Perhaps no one knows more about that than the minister, because he was in an institution which had a great deal to do with teaching regarding this very matter. I refer to what is known as the school of technology, I think it is the Massachusetts school of technology, one of the foremost institutions in the world; they had to do with the mechanical side of business; but across the way, in the great university, the question of transportation was enagaging the attention of very brilliant minds, and at last the Interstate Commerce Commission came into being. Here Mr. Blair, having deputed Mr. McLean to
make an investigation, put upon our statute books the law which established the railway commission.
There is no inconsistency in our position. I want to make clear to my hon. friend the minister our contention that at this stage of our national life we cannot go back and start again. Disraeli once said that democracy could never retrace its steps. I have a favourite saying that not even heaven itself can change the past; what has been, has been. These words I regard as of tremendous import in the life of nations. Here is this country with all these railways-rightly or wrongly. My hon. friends opposite are responsible for our having three systems. The great Canadian who sat in that chair opposite me told the people of this country that $13,000,000 would pay for the National Transcontinental; and his colleague the Minister of Finance, Mr. Fielding, made the same observation, and they believed it. I am not for a moment saying that they were endeavouring to impress these views upon the Canadian people without believing in them, for they did believe them. We looked into the future; we had great dreams, and we are unable to see them realized.
What we are doing now is endeavouring to start again at scratch. If the minister had said, when we were duplicating existing facilities, "I am going to insist upon a licence being granted before that facility is duplicated," we would have had a different situation. If the minister will take the trouble to read the debates on the Grand Trunk Pacific and the amendment of the late Sir Robert Borden with respect to the construction of the line from the head of the lakes eastward, he will see that had that amendment been adopted we should not have had what we have now; we should not be faced with our present difficulties in connection with these various systems. I mention that not by way of argument but to indicate some of the difficulties there are ;n retracing our steps. The minister knows, when he speaks about that map on the wall with black tape on five thousand miles, that we cannot retrace our steps and cancel five thousand miles of track. Everybody knows that. A method by which it may not be served as it has been in days past is another thing altogether, whether it should be treated as a secondary or tertiary line or in some other manner. Some lines can be taken up, but to talk about blacking out five thousand miles is another matter altogether. I do not believe it is possible for us at this time to retrace our steps in the matter of transportation. I do not think the minister has recognized the

consistency which runs through our position, or perhaps I should say my own position, because I do not say that it represents anyone but myself, and I speak for myself only. Licences should be granted in the public interest for the safety and convenience of the individuals who may be passengers on the ship, or for the rapid conveyance of the goods the ship carries; or second, the purpose may be to destroy competition. That was the point which the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) made. The minister, I am sure, has studied and realizes that open competition on the high seas has been the regulating factor in connection with ocean freights, notwithstanding cartels or tramp arrangements and everything of that sort; the sudden introduction into a harbour of a tramp flying a Scandinavian flag, or the flag of Germany or of some other mercantile power, has had the effect of adjusting freights at once. We know that in Montreal; we know it in Vancouver, and we know it in other parts of the world. That is the view to which I find it difficult to accommodate myself.
One more statement and I have concluded. I have trespassed too much on the patience of this committee. The consistency of my position lies in the fact that I maintain there should be equality under the law for all persons who have voyages to make or freight to ship; that is, that the tolls which are fixed by law should be of universal application, fixed by a body which is free from political control, as the board of railway commissioners set up by Hon. Mr. Blair was, he himself being the first chairman; and that that board's rates should be of universal application.
I wonder whether the minister remembers the case that was tested as to whether or not a freight rate was in the nature of a toll or tariff; having once been approved by the body which had to give its approval, no lower rate could be taken nor could a greater sum be exacted; and if a mistake were made the money could be recovered, because there is no power to alter a toll for freight which stood in the same position as a tariff. I once defended an action-unsuccessfully-from that angle. I point out that the really fundamental principle which has governed us for over thirty years has been equality under the law with respect to tolls and charges for the transport of goods in this country, and that no discrimination was possible and no differentiation by reason of the volume of traffic that the shipper had to offer to the carrier.
I ask that that principle be retained, and I submit that to exact a licence with the conditions to be imposed regarding an agreed charge is an inroad on that principle. When the minister suggests that I am favourable or anyone else is favourable to the relaxation of the rule, he has failed to understand the position we take. I am in favour of the maintenance of the principle I have enunciated, and I am opposed to any statutory provision which encroaches upon the application of that principle. The minister says that this does not interfere with it; but I say that any agreed charge, the benefit of which is not open to any man to receive, whether the traffic he has to offer be large or small, is not sound in principle. And the agreed charge contemplates that a man is going to tie himself up to a given condition for a given time in order that he may be able to secure a given rate. That, I submit, is contrary to the principle which I think should continue in effect in this country.
Without going into details, because the matter has been threshed out by so many members of the committee, although of course the jurisdiction of this general committee is still complete and we have the. right to discuss it in any detail we please, I do not propose to enter into any further discussion with respect to general principles. I content myself merely by saying that I think it is a retrograde movement. If we were going to start de novo, I am not sure that I would not be in favour of the general application of a principle that utilizes the accumulated knowledge, scientific and otherwise, and the skill of mankind for the benefit of the citizens of this country as a whole. To think by legislation to turn back the hands of the clock and put ourselves in the position we

Transport Commission

were in when we started in this transportation business is, of course, not for a moment to be considered. Under these circumstances it is the inconsistency of our position that I present for the consideration of the minister, and I do submit that to license vessels which carry people from one part of Canada to another, not for purposes of safety, not for purposes of their well-being, not for purposes of expedition in the handling of freight but for another reason altogether, is contrary to the general principle upon which nations have built up their positions as commercial communities, and I believe will be detrimental to the best interests of the country as a whole.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to labour the discussion on part II of the bill. I intend later on to speak more fully to another part; but I should like to say in regard to part II, which deals with transport by water, that I think it is an unwise policy to adopt to bring this shipping under the board, and to restrict, control and regulate in the manner proposed in the bill. I shall state in a few sentences why I take that position.
One of our major items of export, as well as one of our chief sources of new wealth, is found of course in the great wheat plains of the west. The handicap to which the Canadian wheat producer is subject is that his product is produced at a point a couple of thousand miles away from the seaboard. We are in competition chiefly with the Argentine, as well as with other countries, of course. But the Argentine wheat is the closest competitor to Canadian wheat. The Argentine grower virtually has water transportation at his door. Therefore anything that affects or is likely to affect the cost of the movement of grain from the western plains to the seaboard is a matter which should be very carefully considered by parliament.
This is not a new proposal by any means. It was introduced to the house very frequently in years gone by. Almost every year it was placed before the house by the hon. member
51952-225$
who at that time represented Lambton. On every occasion I opposed it, and the bill which was introduced year after year did not become law, not because I alone opposed' it but because parliament in its wisdom decided it was not advisable to impose restrictions upon shipping on the great lakes, because of the danger of affecting the cost of transportation on those lakes.
There is no need of subterfuge or evading the issue, and parliament ought to face the facts that the only possible effect of part II of the bill would be to raise the cost of transportation on the great lakes. That is its object; there is not any question about it.

In the interpretation clause of the bill we have outlined a distinct and absolute limitation as to the goods which may be carried by bulk carriers which are not necessarily licensed under the bill. The rights are definitely limited, because we have forbidden them from carrying any goods other than those mentioned in paragraph (e) which reads:
"Goods in bulk" means the following goods laden or freighted in ships, and except as herein otherwise provided, not bundled or enclosed in bags, bales, boxes, cases, sacks, crates or any other container;
grain and grain products, including flour and mill feeds in sacks,
ores and minerals (crude, screened, sized, refined or concentrated, but not otherwise processed), including ore concentrates in sacks,
coal and coke,
liquids.
The bulk carrier in the past has moved *grain to ports such as Montreal and Quebec, and has been at liberty to pick up any kind of cargo in any quantity he wished, on a return trip. It is well known that the vessel hauling grain down there desires as quickly as possible to return to the head of the lakes in order to secure another load of grain eastward. The consequence of that method of movement was that they did pick up cargoes, sometimes only small portions and sometimes cargoes of a substantial size, on return trips. The more cargo they secured going west, the lower would be the rate on grain coming east. We are definitely restricting that. What I said a moment ago, to which the minister took exception, was that the committee ought to be fully seized of the effect of this part of the bill before it is finally passed.
I took this stand in the committee. It is true the bill passed the committee, but I now submit to the committee of the whole house that merely because a standing committee passed the bill is no reason why it should be passed here without discussion. The bill should be fully discussed; the committee should be seized of the import of it, and the possible effect it may have. In part II we propose to license ships on the great lakes and certain other ships running from the Pacific coast to the great lakes. These ships are to be licensed; they are to be restricted, and such ships as are not licensed are forbidden to carry certain cargoes westward on the great lakes, which at present they are privileged to carry.
Let me give one illustration of the far-reaching effect of this bill. One of the main items of cargo moving westward is sugar. Sugar is something that affects the livelihood of every person in western Canada. A certain part of western Canada is supplied with its

sugar requirements from the Pacific coast. I believe the Pacific coast refineries reach eastward as far as Regina.

That portion of the population of western Canada living between Port Arthur and Regina secures its sugar supplies via the great lakes. We are now prohibiting the bulk carrier moving grain eastward from taking cargoes of sugar west-ivard, unless he complies with the regulated rates. As a regulated carrier he would have to file a tariff and comply with the rates under the direction of the board. Sugar is only one of many items.
My purpose in raising this point was to call the attention of the committee to this part of the bill and to register my objection to the regulation of traffic on the great lakes. The inevitable result will be to raise the rates, generally speaking, for the movement of goods eastward as well as westward on the great lakes. I think that is something of very grave importance to this country.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIR CRAFT
speechtext: I take exception with my hon. friend when he says that the effect of this bill will be to raise rates. In my opinion the effect of the bill will be to create a more efficient transportation system in Canada. As I said previously this evening, an efficient transportation system is less costly to operate. The people who pay the cost of operating our transportation systems are not the owners, they are the usere of transportation. If we can reduce transportation costs by a more effective coordination of the various forms of transportation, we shall be benefiting the users of transportation. I do not think anyone will contend that regulation has increased the cost of railway transportation. I think it is quite obvious that by bringing order out of chaos in the way of rates, the cost of railway transportation has been somewhat reduced. My hon. friend seems to be the defender of everybody from the needleworker to the Montreal brokers. I suppose he is now the defender of the people against a government that are trying to increase transportation costs. There is nothing in this bill that justifies the position he is taking in that regard.

I consider it as about the highest compliment that has been paid to me since I have been in the House of Commons to be called the defender of the needleworkers of Canada.
The minister attempts to brush the whole question aside by drawing a parallel between railway and water transportation. No student of transportation would for a moment accept such an analogy. There is no parallel at all between the two. The essence of sound policy in connection with water transportation from its earliest days down to the present has been freedom from control and direction and restriction. Freedom of the seas! The movement of freight on our inland lakes is virtually the same as the movement of freight across the seas. There is no difference between the two except that geographically the lakes happen to be within the territory of the United States and Canada, while the seas are open to all. In so far as the movement of goods by water is concerned, our inland lakes do not differ from the seas in any particular. As I said a moment ago,, the essence of the policy down through the ages has been to keep water-borne transportation as free as possible from restriction and regulation. There is no parallel between the two.
My hon. friend said a moment ago that no one would suggest that the regulation of rail tx-affic has resulted in increased freight l-ates. If one examines the schedule of rates, his answer certainly will be disconcerting to the minister, because, generally speaking, freight rates are higher to-day than they were before the introduction of regulation. But that argument is not applicable to the case at all. I am not suggesting that the regulation of railway rates was improvident or unwise. The chaos that existed then is the very chaos which will exist if part V of this bill is put into force. What were the chaotic conditions that existed prior to the regulation by the board of railway commissioners in 1905? Then the railways were competing with one another. They were making secret rebates and giving special rates, to favoured shippers and all that sort of thing. They were failing to supply the public with the proper facilities for loading and unloading goods at different points along their systems. But all of that was changed. All of that chaos was wiped out by the regulation of the railways. There is no parallel between that and waterborne transportation.
We might as well be frank about this. As far as the ship owners are concerned, this is
being done for the Canada Steamship company alone. The minister knows perfectly well that pi-actically all the other shipping concerns on the great lakes opposed this part of the bill. I should like to see it prosper, but I think it is unwise for parliament to pass legislation that will benefit this one company alone and be detrimental to other shipping concerns. In my opinion this legislation will tend to increase rates generally on the movement of grain eastward to seaboard points.

I think the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) has perhaps not made the point quite clear. Speaking for myself, I do not object to the exemption of the maritime provinces from this measure; in fact I supported it very strongly in the committee. The point is this: In recent years, say the last twelve years or thereabouts, we have developed an inter-coastal trade between Pacific coast ports and eastern Canadian ports, Montreal and places on the great lakes. The history of that is very interesting and important. Prior to the introduction of that service, which was inaugurated originally by the Canadian National Steamships, supplies for British Columbia came very largely from the eastern United States and Europe. By the introduction of this intercoastal service a great deal of that business, that is, manufactured goods, was diverted to eastern Canada, Ontario and Quebec. Then, because of high rail freight rates, we were not able to ship lumber into eastern Canada to compete with southern pine from the United States. After the introduction of that service, however, we moved lumber from the Pacific coast to the east, and we took back
Transport Commission

manufactured goods; steel, sugar, etc. I saw a manifest the other day with, I think, forty different items on it from eastern Canada to the west. That is distinctly in the interest of building up trade within Canada.
The service was inugurated by the Canadian National Steamships and subsequently was taken over by Mr. MacMillan's company, which has maintained it ever since without any subsidy or assistance of any kind. Under this bill that service is brought into regulation. The reason that exemption was not included in the bill is that those who operate the service made no objection to being regulated, and I did not press the point. But they do object-and I am going to refer to it later-to the agreed charges part. There is a vital point there affecting their interests. But as far as this particular part is concerned, my view is that they would be better if they were not regulated; for it is obvious that a service running eight or ten thousand miles from British Columbia ports around through the Panama canal and up the St. Lawrence to the great lakes is not a local service, because the major part of it is a sea voyage; but my position in the committee was that, inasmuch as the operators of the service did not press to be exempted, I did not myself insist on the point. I would, however, submit to my hon. friend that the maritime provinces case should not be brought into comparison, because that stands on its own footing, and I think they had a perfect right to claim the exemption which they received.

speechtext:
I had intended to make some rather extended observations with re-

Supply-National Defence-Administration
spect to the administration of the Department of National Defence, but at this hour of the evening I shall not endeavour to do so. However, I shall deal with this matter when the supply bill is under consideration and an opportunity is afforded for discussion. But there is one matter that I must bring to the attention of the committee to-night. This concerns the right of a deputy minister, because he occupies a position of importance, to libel a citizen of this country.
The department called for tenders for coal at Kingston. Tenders were submitted by Drury's, Crawford's, Norman's, the Morris coal company, and also by the firm of James Sowards company. Their tender was the lowest, whereupon the deputy minister advised the minister that the acceptance of the lowest tender, that of James Sowards company, was not recommended because of reports received concerning this firm. The minister passed on that information in his order in council and it became part of the permanent records of this country. I should like to know just what those reports are. Mr. Sowards is a large taxpayer and a reputable citizen. He does not support the government of the country; at the present moment he is a supporter of the opposition, and has been for some time. He made his tender, which was the lowest tender by thousands of dollars, and the deputy minister advised his minister not to accept that tender because, to quote his words, "of reports received concerning this firm." I have here the return in my hand. I have shown the return to Mr. Sowards. As a citizen of equal reputation with the deputy minister at least, he demands the right to know what those reports were that prevented the taxpayers of Canada from being relieved of a burden of many thousands of dollars. What right had the deputy minister to take this action? What right had any man in that position to do it? And that is only one of about twenty similar proceedings which I desire to discuss. The minister, of course, must assume responsibility for these things, as he does, because he passes them along; but when it is recorded that the deputy minister recommends such and such a thing, I rather doubt the right of any deputy minister to be the controlling factor in the language here used:
The minister, on the advice of the deputy minister of National Defence, recommends that the tender of Messrs. Morris Coal Company, be accepted as follows:
1,000	tons bituminous run of mine coal, "Yatesboro" at $6.60 ton.
100 tons coke, nut size, "Hamilton or LaSalle" at $12 ton.
Acceptance of the lowest tender, that of Messrs. James Sowards Coal Company is not recommended because of reports received concerning this firm.
That is part of the public records, and Mr. Sowards wants to know what those reports are. That is one of many matters in which the deputy minister, either of his own volition or under pressure, has become the instrument of political oppression. It applies to individuals; it applies to firms; it applies to contracts. Whether or not he did this of his own volition, it is for the minister to say, and whether or not he reflected the mind of the minister and the administration when he made this statement. But it is my duty to ask why a citizen should be pilloried in this way by any person who finds himself in a position of brief authority.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIR CRAFT
speechtext:
I have not the documents before me at the moment with reference to the particular tender mentioned by the right hon. gentleman, but I definitely recall that complaints were made in regard to the carrying out of a previous contract by this same gentleman, with reference to a definite breach of the labour conditions in the contract. I shall ascertain the exact terms of the complaint and shall be glad to supply it to my right hon. friend or to any member of the committee.
In view of my right hon. friend's references to the deputy minister, I wish to say immediately that the minister of the department assumes full and complete responsibility for every action by the department, and I wish also to say immediately that in my whole experience there is not to be found in the public service of Canada a gentleman more devoted to his duty and more self-sacrificing in the execution of his duty than the deputy minister of National Defence. I know personally that he toils far into the night, probably at a great sacrifice of his own health, and I submit to the right hon. gentleman, with the utmost deference, that he has been misinformed with reference to this matter.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIR CRAFT
speechtext: I am reading from a public document.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIR CRAFT
speechtext:
I submit to my right hon. friend that what he has read from that record will be substantiated, and that it does not refer in the slightest degree to the deputy minister of National Defence. I do not recall the exact circumstances, but very likely instructions came from the minister to the deputy. I shall be glad to look up the exact details and back up what I say
3558	COMMONS
Supply-National Defence-Administration
because this is probably the only case in which the lowest tender has been refused in the department for the last two and a half years. I wish to state that there has never been an inquiry from the deputy minister to me of the slightest political significance, and that I have never seen a deputy minister more courteous to the members of this house of all shades of political opinion. The members of the opposition receive the same courteous treatment from him as do the supporters of this administration, and I regret very much that the right hon. gentleman saw fit to make the remarks that he did. I can assure him in reference to the contract he has mentioned that the information will be supplied to justify the statement made in that memorandum.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIR CRAFT
speechtext: The minister has entirely failed to appreciate the point that I made. He has seen fit to make a recommendation to council based upon a recommendation made to him by the deputy minister, which provided for the acceptance of a tender that was not the lowest, which lowest tender was declined because, it was stated, "of reports received concerning this firm." Did the minister take any steps to ascertain whether they were correct or not? Did he give the man an opportunity to make an answer? Did he communicate with him at all?

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIR CRAFT
speechtext: No.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIR CRAFT
speechtext: No, and that is British justice. Right there in black and white is a document impugning the reputation of a firm that enjoys at least as good a reputation as the deputy minister, and he attacks it and gives no reason for it, and does not communicate with the man. Why? This gentleman could not get a set of the tender forms, not being on the list of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) and not being able to get the forms, he puts in his tender and says: " I will fill out any form you require." The director of contracts felt that he could not deal with the situation, and so the minister says: "Do not accept the lowest tender; he happens to be a Conservative."

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIR CRAFT
speechtext: That is not. correct. It had nothing to do with it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIR CRAFT
speechtext: Where is that stated, that he is a Conservative.

subtopic: AUTHORITY TO CONTROL TRANSPORT OF PASSENGERS AND GOODS BY RAILWAYS, SHIPS AND AIR CRAFT
speechtext:
I will tell you where it is stated. It is stated right in the document where his tender was refused-not in terms, but that was the reason. I will show you his
 '
letter. He did not have a set of the forms sent to him. Oh, no, that was not done. But he wrote to the department:
Sewards Coal,
Kingston, Ontario,
June 26, 1937.
We the undersigned are prepared to supply the department at Kingston and Barriefield with coal and coke at the following prices:
Then follow the prices, and the letter concludes:
We w'ill fill in regular form if supplied with same.
Yours truly,
James Sowards Coal Company, per J. F. Sowards.
There was no objection made to the fact that the tender was not on the regular form. No forms were sent to him to fill in. But the deputy minister, according to this document- the minister says he has no recollection of the circumstances at the moment-advised the minister that the tender of Messrs. Morris Coal Company be accepted, and that:
Acceptance of the lowest tender, that of Messrs. James Sowards Coal Company, is not recommended because of reports received concerning this firm.
The taxpayers of this country have had to pay thousands of dollars more for their coal, and no opportunity was afforded to Mr. Sowards to meet the anonymous assassin who stabs him in the back without giving him a chance to defend himself. And this is typical of the administration. The Minister of Labour is not in his place, but if the Minister of National Defence will apply to him he will get. some information about the matter.
